analysis.one_liner: Cuts the EPA's workforce by 15% within three years.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the EPA workforce by 15% never received a hearing or vote in any of its four committees and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Environmental Protection Agency to shrink its staff by 15% within three years of enactment, with the Administrator reporting to Congress on compliance and allowed to delay the deadline by up to one year. The bill's findings argue EPA staff and rulemaking have grown and that its rules are costly to the economy. A smaller EPA staff means fewer inspectors, scientists, and enforcement attorneys working on air and water pollution rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by the EPA — fossil fuel producers, power plants, manufacturers, and other polluters — would face a smaller workforce enforcing the rules that apply to them, which typically means fewer inspections and slower enforcement actions. Taxpayers would save the salary costs of the cut positions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA Administrator to ensure the agency's total employee count three years after enactment does not exceed the baseline count reduced by 15% [S2] [S3].
Requires written reports to Congress on the baseline headcount, compliance, and any deadline extensions of up to one year [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities exposed to air and water pollution would bear the cost of reduced oversight: fewer EPA staff means fewer inspections, slower cleanups, and less capacity to write and enforce health standards. EPA employees would lose their jobs, and federal employees generally would face a precedent for mandated headcount cuts.

drawbacks.text: A flat 15% headcount cut applies regardless of which functions are cut, so enforcement and scientific work could shrink without any assessment of which programs matter most; the bill sets a staffing target rather than identifying waste [S3].

The bill's economic case rests on its own findings — including a claim that EPA compliance cost the economy $353 billion in 2012 "according to one study" — which the bill presents without independent verification [S3].

Supporters would argue that EPA staffing grew 107% from 1972 to 2011 while total federal personnel fell 15%, and that 95% of EPA employees were deemed non-essential during the 2013 shutdown, justifying a smaller workforce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a simple taxpayer saving and a smaller regulatory workforce, but its design is blunt: an across-the-board percentage cut gives the agency no flexibility to protect core functions like drinking-water safety or toxic-site cleanups. For ordinary people, the trade is reduced federal pollution oversight in exchange for modest federal savings, with the enforcement burden effectively shifted onto states and individuals.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2013 and referred to four House committees, but no committee ever held a hearing or vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith introduced the bill on December 3, 2013 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Science, Space, and Technology — and then to subcommittees in each [S1] [S5].

No further action was taken after the subcommittee referrals in December 2013, and the bill never received a committee markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: EPA employees kept their jobs, and communities relying on federal air and water enforcement were spared a 15% smaller regulator; the regulated industries that would have benefited from a reduced workforce gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited co-sponsors

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Science, Space, and Technology
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral; no committee action occurred after December 2013

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven co-sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat supported it; no votes were ever taken to test broader support [S4] [S1].

industries.industry: Polluting industries regulated by the EPA (fossil fuels, power generation, manufacturing)
industries.note: A 15% smaller EPA workforce would mean fewer inspections, slower enforcement, and reduced rulemaking capacity — the very functions that constrain these industries. The industry's gain (less oversight) is the public's cost (weaker pollution control) [S2] [S3].
About 15% of EPA positions would have been eliminated within three years [S2] [S3].
Salary and overhead costs of eliminated positions would be saved, though the savings are small relative to the agency's overall budget and the public loses the corresponding oversight capacity [S3].
